title: Senior's toolkit: patterns the .NET container gives you
summary: Strategies, factories, decorators, observers and options as you actually write them in a .NET app.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: patterns the .NET container gives you
steps.body: In a modern .NET app you rarely hand-write a pattern from the book. The dependency injection container, events and the options system already do most of it; knowing their APIs is what lets you apply a pattern in five lines.

toolkit.what: Keyed services (.NET 8+): several implementations of one interface, chosen by a key. A strategy picked by name, with no switch statement.
flags: the usual lifetimes, plus a key
ask for a keyed service in a constructor or endpoint parameter
resolve by a key known only at run time

toolkit.what: Register several implementations without keys and inject `IEnumerable<T>` to get all of them, in registration order. The simplest way to run every rule or every channel.
A factory registration: you decide how the object is built. Use it to wrap one implementation in another (a decorator) or to pass settings in.
flags: a lambda that receives the container
resolve the pieces you are wrapping

toolkit.what: Decorators in one line with **Scrutor**, a popular third-party package (not part of .NET). It replaces the registration with your wrapper around the original.
flags: stack another decorator on the outside
Scrutor's other feature: register types by convention

toolkit.what: The observer pattern built into C#. Subscribers add handlers; the owner raises the event without knowing who listens.
flags: subscribe / unsubscribe; forgetting `-=` keeps the subscriber alive
raise it safely when nobody subscribed
synchronously, one after another, on the raising thread

toolkit.what: The options pattern: bind a settings section to a class, validate it, inject it. Configuration stops leaking into every class as raw strings.
flags: fail at start-up, not at the first request
read once / per request / with live reload

steps.prompt: You switched the notifiers to `AddKeyedSingleton<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")`. Now a request fails with this. Why?
steps.code: System.InvalidOperationException: Unable to resolve service for type 'INotifier' while attempting to activate 'Alerts'.
options: A keyed registration is invisible to a plain `INotifier` parameter; `Alerts` must ask for `[FromKeyedServices("sms")] INotifier`
`Alerts` must be registered as keyed too
Keys must be enums, not strings
steps.explain: Keyed and unkeyed registrations are separate. Either keep an unkeyed default registration as well, or have each consumer say which key it wants.

steps.prompt: Match each options interface to how it behaves.
pairs: read once, the same value for the app's lifetime

steps.prompt: Register an email notifier under the key "email" and ask for it in a constructor.
code: public sealed class Receipts([__2__("email")] INotifier notifier) { }
steps.explain: `AddSingleton` has no key parameter. `[FromServices]` is the MVC attribute for unkeyed services; keyed ones need `[FromKeyedServices]`.

steps.prompt: Two observers subscribe to the same event. What does this print?
steps.explain: Handlers run synchronously in the order they subscribed. If the first one throws, the second never runs: one reason a message bus or a `Channel` is used when observers must be isolated.

items: Use the payment provider named in config (`"stripe"` or `"adyen"`)
Send through the channel the user picked, by name
Run every validation rule on an order
Notify through every channel that is registered
Log every call to `INotifier` without editing the notifiers
Retry failed sends of one provider

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When you are about to write a `switch` that picks an implementation, reach for keyed services or `IEnumerable<T>`. When you want to add logging, caching or retries around something, write a decorator and register it, instead of editing the class. Read settings through validated options, never through raw configuration strings.
